newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Political and financial pundits poles apart on HK.
newsitem.headline: Political and financial pundits poles apart on HK.

text.p: Stock market players and risk analysts are giving Hong Kong a big thumbs-up in sharp contrast to political pundits who predict disaster and tyranny after China takes back the British colony on July 1.

The stock market soared into uncharted heavens on Wednesday, when the Hang Seng Index closed above the magic 14,000 barrier for the first time, boosted by an upgrade in ratings on China and Hong Kong by Standard & Poor's.

"The market often has a clearer and simpler understanding of the realities of political risk in Hong Kong," Richard Margolis, First Vice President of Merrill Lynch (Asia Pacific) Ltd, told Reuters on Thursday.
"Trends in the Hang Seng Index have never been determined by politics," Margolis said.

The huge financial vote of confidence came a day before post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa unveiled draft legislation that will curtail some of Hong Kong's political liberties after the sovereignty change. The curbs have fanned a political storm.
Tung on Thursday announced modifications to the planned curbs but the basic principles of restricting foreign political funding in Hong Kong and preventing anti-China protests remained unaltered.

Ratings agency S&P lifted its ratings on China and Hong Kong, saying broad support in China for economic liberalisation after leader Deng Xiaoping's death in February and progress in fiscal and financial reforms had prompted it to review China's sovereign credit ratings in a more positive light.
Hong Kong's long-term rating was raised simultaneously, based on the agency's belief that the territory would enjoy great autonomy under China from July 1, less than 50 days away.
The moves boosted ratings on companies in China and Hong Kong, and fuelled a surge in the stock market.
The optimism was sharply at odds with the raging political debate over Hong Kong's future this week.
"The substance of the issue on human rights doesn't justify the amount of fuss being made about it," said Margolis.

In a war of rival legislatures, pro-democracy politicians in the elected Legislative Council failed on Wednesday night to push through a motion of censure on Tung's proposals to curb protest rights and foreign funding of political groups.

The motion was defeated by pro-China forces in the chamber by 27 to 23. Tung plans to send the draft legislation on Saturday to an appointed shadow legislature operating over the border in China that will replace the elected council on July 1.
Legislator Margaret Ng attacked the curbs as a move that could lead to tyranny. "Such a mentality, beginning perhaps in goodwill, inevitably leads to tyranny."
"For civil liberties are there not only to protect the individuals, but to protect society from becoming enslaved by a few," Ng said.

Ng's arguments in the debate reflect the widely held view promoted by pro-democracy groups such as Martin Lee's Democratic Party that China will snuff out democracy and impose repressive rule by scrapping the elected legislature as its first step.

Tung's future Justice Secretary Elsie Leung admitted trust in the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) government was thin. "Concerns and worries arose mainly because some people didn't have much confidence in the SAR government," she told reporters.
Under a 1984 Sino-British treaty, Hong Kong, after 156 years as a colony, will become a quasi-autonomous region within China, free to run all its own affairs except defence and diplomacy.
